source.title: Mathematical Models of Computation in Superposition
source.authors: Kaarel Hänni; Jake Mendel; Dmitry Vaintrob; Lawrence Chan

page_placements.theme: Capacity limits and computation in superposition (theory and constructions)

record.tranche_reason: The paper gives theoretical constructions and guarantees about computing sparse Boolean features in superposition, rather than measuring polysemantic neurons in trained models.
record.gate_note: The paper's own theorem results on representing and computing Boolean features in superposition are included. Statements about polysemantic neurons and results cited from other work are not rows; the paper does not experimentally measure individual neuron responses.
record.test_reason: This is a purely theoretical paper. It proves that ReLU MLPs can compute sparse Boolean circuits (U-AND and general sparse circuits) with fewer neurons than computed features. It cites polysemanticity and the superposition hypothesis as motivation. It never measures neuron responses in any trained model, and it does not show that observed polysemantic neurons are caused by superposition. Existence and capacity proofs, including the random-initialization theorem, show the mechanism is possible, not that V3 holds for real networks. So no row measures what any version names.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors give a mathematical framework showing networks can emulate sparse Boolean circuits entirely in superposition, with outputs far outnumbering neurons. They also argue that randomly initialized networks likely emulate U-AND, so real networks may implement the construction. They draw interpretability takeaways: SAE dictionaries of roughly d² features, alternative SAE nonlinearities, and caution that linearly probeable features may be unused. They stress limits: binary features, sparsity assumptions, and their choice of representation definition.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses mathematical constructions and asymptotic proofs for sparse Boolean circuits, rather than the original sources' neuron visualization or SoLU methods.

fits_no_version.finding: Constructed and randomly initialized ReLU MLPs can epsilon-linearly represent and compute far more Boolean features (e.g. all m-choose-2 pairwise ANDs, circuits of width about d^1.5) than they have neurons, given sparse inputs. In these constructions each neuron reads a random subset of features, unlike naive one-neuron-per-AND 'monosemantic' implementations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Computation in superposition is theoretically possible: sparse-feature networks can compute more features than neurons, with features distributed across many neurons.

record.peer_reviewed: Presented at the inaugural Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at ICML 2024; peer-review status not stated
record.problems: The evidence is theoretical and asymptotic, concerns Boolean features and sparse inputs, and does not establish that trained real-world networks have polysemantic neurons for this reason. The paper notes that sparsity in real networks is uncertain and that its chosen notion of feature representation may need revision.

untested.parts: Whether polysemantic neurons in trained networks arise because more sparse features than neurons are packed together. The paper only proves such packing is possible.
All: the paper discusses feature-representation definitions (weak, epsilon-linear, ReLU-linear), not neuron polysemanticity measurement.

record.verdict_notes: The reader labelled this T2 'tests' with a V3 'supports' verdict. I downgrade it: theorems showing superposition is possible do not test whether observed polysemantic neurons are caused by it. A lenient reading could treat the constructions as theoretical plausibility support for V3. Even then, no trained network is examined. All rows are theorem statements, not measurements.

versions.untested_parts: Transformer language models, MLP neurons, tokens, and layerwise prevalence.
Whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity in trained networks, and whether this mechanism explains real neurons' mixed responses.
Polysemanticity when there are enough neurons for every feature; initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of such polysemanticity.
Comparisons across activations, architectures, or regularization, including SoLU or modern convnets, and performance costs.
Whether apparently mixed neuron responses share a coherent feature or job.
How neuron polysemanticity varies with activation range or explanation-scoring method.

rows.uncertainty: Theorem guarantee; probability qualifier not stated

rows.check: Existence construction with inputs in superposition. This is a capacity result, not a measurement of neuron polysemanticity or its cause.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: Cites polysemanticity and the superposition hypothesis as motivation (Introduction) and discusses implications (Appendix B), but does not test them.

tranche.reason: Purely theoretical existence and random-initialization results on computing Boolean circuits in superposition. No neuron polysemanticity is measured in any trained model, so no version is tested.

source_check.notes: All seven rows match the theorem statements: asymptotic existence or random-initialization guarantees (Õ, 'outside negligible probability'), with no neuron-level evidence on any version. Inside the paper, the abstract and Figure 1 give Õ(m^{2/3}) neurons for U-AND with superposed inputs, but Theorem 2 states Õ(√m/ε²).

statements.correction: Text supports this. Theorems 1-2: U-AND (all m-choose-2 pairwise ANDs) with width polylog(m)/ε² (basis-aligned inputs) or Õ(√m/ε²) (inputs in superposition). Theorems 3 and 14: randomly initialized Gaussian ReLU layers ε-linearly represent pairwise ANDs outside negligible probability. Abstract and Theorem 8: deep constructed networks of width d emulate circuits of width Õ(d^1.5). The d^1.5 result covers constructed networks only, not random init. Theory only.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Theoretical sparse-Boolean constructions and the stated random-initialization setting
reader_labels.reason: The constructions show that more Boolean outputs than hidden dimensions can be represented and computed in superposition; the random-initialization theorem gives a related guarantee for U-AND (thm1, thm2, thm3, cor4, thm6, thm8, thm14).
